title: Fake news on Twitter during the 2016 U.S. presidential election
screen_reason: Behavioural panel study (16,442 registered-voter Twitter accounts linked to voter files, 1 Aug - 6 Dec 2016) reporting the share of political-URL exposures and shares coming from fake news sources, per-person exposure intensity, the share of political sharers who ever shared fake news, and explicit user- and source-level concentration figures.

estimates.value_raw: 5.0% of aggregate exposures to political URLs
estimates.denominator: All aggregate exposures to political URLs among the 16,442-account voter-linked Twitter panel (a tweet from an account followed by five panel members counted five times)

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Fig. 3 reports the percent of each political-affinity subgroup with NONZERO exposure to fake news sources (extreme left 78%, N=1386; left 74%, N=6011; center 67%, N=2195; right 71%, N=2609; extreme right 78%, N=570). These are genuine REACH figures but no pooled panel-wide REACH value is reported, and computing the weighted average across subgroups would violate R8, so no REACH row was created. An adjudicator may want the five subgroup rows. 2) The red (2.4%) and orange (1.9%) exposure sub-shares are verbatim but are non-cumulative components of the 5.0% total, not alternative definitions, so only the black (0.7%) strict variant got its own row. 3) '...this would translate to, on average, about 10 exposures (95% CI: 9 to 11) to fake news sources during that month' is conditional on the untested assumption that 5% of potential exposures are seen; not extracted as a value. 4) Share of websites in each coexposure cluster that are fake news sources (Group 2: 68.8%; Group 1: 3.6%; Group 3: 2.0%; Group 4: 11.4%) - denominators are algorithmically derived network clusters rather than a defined population of sites, so not extracted. 5) 'Of the 7484 nonoutlier panel members exposed to at least two fake news URLs, 95.6% of them saw URLs from at least two fake news sources, and 56.4% encountered URLs from at least five' measures source diversity within the already-exposed, not prevalence. 6) 'fewer than 5% of people on the left or in the center ever shared any fake news content' is a bound over two merged subgroups, so no row. 7) Group 1 (mainstream) share of political exposures by affinity (72% extreme right to 86% extreme left) is a non-misinformation quantity. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a -layout rendering of a multi-column print page, so the printed sentences are interleaved with the neighbouring columns and no full sentence is contiguous in the file; each source_quote is therefore the exact within-line column fragment carrying the value, and the full sentence is reproduced in value_raw / measure_type.

rob.design: Panel of 16,442 Twitter accounts linked to US public voter-registration records (via TargetSmart), active 1 August - 6 December 2016; demographic comparison against a Pew representative sample of US voters on Twitter reported as broadly matching on age, gender, race and political affiliation. Exposure was not observed directly: each panel member's feed composition was ESTIMATED from a random sample of tweets posted by their followees, so 'exposures' are potential, not verified impressions. Analysis restricted to political tweets containing an external URL. Misinformation coded at the SOURCE (publisher) level via three lists - 171 'black' sites from preexisting fact-checker/journalist/academic lists, 64 'red' and 65 'orange' sites added by manual annotation of Snopes-flagged sites - with no inter-annotator reliability statistic in the main text. Supersharer/superconsumer outliers (top 1%) set aside for individual-level analyses because some were likely partially automated 'cyborg' accounts. No response rate applies (behavioural data); IRB-approved; replication data on Zenodo.
rob.item6_quote: We follow Lazer et al. (13), who defined fake news outlets as those that have the trappings of legitimately produced news but "lack the news media's editorial norms and processes for ensuring the accuracy and credibility of information." The attribution of "fakeness" is thus not at the level of the story but at that of the publisher [similar to (9)].
rob.item10_quote: When totaled across all panel members and the entire 2016 U.S. election season, 5.0% of aggregate exposures to political URLs were from fake news sources.
